meta.description: No. The line pinned on IBM’s Thomas J. Watson has no source — no speech, no document, and print versions that disagree on 1943 vs 1958.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I think there is a world market for maybe five computers'?
meta.ogDescription: Thomas J. Watson never documentably said it. The real remark: his son, in 1953, expected five orders for the IBM 701 and came home with 18.

answer.label: Not Thomas J. Watson — an unsourced legend
answer.authorDates: No speaker on record · the line appears in no Watson speech, paper or contemporary article
answer.sourceLine: No primary source exists. Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed ↗, noting that thorough research of Watson’s writings and statements has produced no example of him saying it, and Wikipedia records that biographer Kevin Maney — author of the 2003 Watson Sr. biography — could find no speech, document or contemporary article containing the words. The dates attached to it float between 1943 and 1958, which is itself a sign that no one is working from a record.

author.name: Thomas J. Watson
author.kicker: The man who didn’t say it
author.heading: Who Thomas J. Watson actually was
author.metaLine: 1874–1956 · Head of CTR and then IBM · the man the quote is pinned on
author.bio: Thomas J. Watson Sr. took over the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company in 1914 and renamed it International Business Machines in 1924, running it until shortly before his death in 1956. He is the standard punchline of technology forecasting — the executive who supposedly could not imagine more than five computers — on the strength of a sentence no one has ever traced to him. His actual record is the opposite of the caricature: the company he built spent his final decade pouring money into electronic computing.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the popular version
misattribution.intro: Almost everything attached to this sentence — the speaker, the year, and the wording itself — fails when you look for a source.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Misattributed section, reporting that thorough research of Watson’s writings and statements has produced no example of him saying it. Wikipedia ↗ adds that Kevin Maney, who wrote the 2003 biography of Watson Sr., could find no speech, document or contemporary article containing the words.

The 1986 Usenet signature that spread the quote online dated it to 1943, while Neil Morgan’s May 15, 1985 San Diego Evening Tribune column dated it to 1958, per Wikipedia ↗. Both dates are asserted without a source.

The 1985 newspaper version and the 1986 Usenet version both read “about five computers,” not the “maybe five computers” that circulates today, according to Wikipedia’s ↗ account of the printed attributions.

items.who: Thomas J. Watson Jr., IBM stockholders meeting, April 28, 1953
items.why: Describing the IBM 701, Watson Jr. said “as a result of our trip, on which we expected to get orders for five machines, we came home with orders for 18,” as recorded on Wikipedia’s IBM 701 page ↗. That is a beaten sales forecast, not a prediction about the world.
Wikiquote ↗ suggests the attribution may stem from a remark by Aiken that four or five computers could meet all of the United Kingdom’s computing needs.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody can show that Thomas J. Watson said this. Geek History’s survey ↗ found dozens of sites repeating it and not one citing an original source.

context.heading: Why this one refuses to die
lead: It is the perfect anecdote: the boss of the world’s biggest business-machine company, standing at the door of the computer age, guessing that five would do. It gets used in keynote slides, business-school lectures and think-pieces about the next technology everyone is underestimating. The only missing ingredient is a source.

What the record actually contains is a much duller and more human moment. At IBM’s annual stockholders meeting on April 28, 1953, Thomas J. Watson Jr. was describing the market for the IBM 701 and said that “as a result of our trip, on which we expected to get orders for five machines, we came home with orders for 18.” That is a sales forecast for one expensive machine, beaten by more than three times — a story about underestimating demand, told by the son, not a prophecy of a five-computer world made by the father.
detailsBody: Wikipedia’s survey of the printed record shows the attribution arriving piecemeal. Der Spiegel wrote on May 22, 1965 that Watson had estimated US demand at a maximum of five machines. Christopher Cerf and Victor S. Navasky’s The Experts Speak (1984) carried a version taken from Morgan and Langford’s Facts and Fallacies. On May 15, 1985 Neil Morgan wrote in the San Diego Evening Tribune that Watson “said in 1958: ‘I think there is a world market for about five computers.’” By 1986 a Convex Computer Corporation poster was carrying it in a Usenet signature, now dated 1943.

Two of those printed versions read “about five computers” rather than the “maybe five computers” that circulates today, and they disagree with each other about the year by fifteen years. A quotation with a real source does not drift like that.
context.pull: The number five is real. The sentence around it is not.
